transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, nice to meet you, Doctor. I'm here because... well, ever since my choir friend passed away so suddenly, I just haven't been myself. 

I find myself crying over little things, like looking at the potluck lists. And I get all worked up about phone calls that I used to handle easy. I've even started missing church planning meetings... and I never would have missed those before. I just feel like I'm having a really hard time managing right now.
How long ago did your friend pass away, and how long have you been feeling this way since then?

Well, she passed away just about a month ago. It was... a very sudden loss. And I've been feeling this way pretty much ever since then. It was really only after she died that I started falling apart with the church planning and everything else. Before that, I was managing just fine.
Over the past month, have you noticed that you feel down or find little interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy, nearly every day, even outside of situations that remind you of your friend?

Well, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean... I still enjoy things when my mind isn't on her. I still like working out in my yard, and I enjoy seeing my family. 

It's not an all-day, every-day kind of sadness about everything in my life. It really just hits me hard when something reminds me of her, or when I have to deal with the church stuff we used to do together. Outside of that, I feel mostly okay.
Besides feeling sad or tearful, have you also been feeling unusually anxious, nervous, or on edge since your friend passed away?

Well, I wouldn't say I've been feeling unusually anxious or nervous, really. It's more just the sadness and getting overwhelmed with the church things. But I don't feel on edge or anything like that in my day-to-day life.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with depressed mood, tearfulness, and functional impairment (missing church planning meetings, difficulty with phone calls) emerging within one month of a clear, identifiable psychosocial stressor (sudden death of a close friend). Symptoms are specifically triggered by reminders of the deceased friend and related activities (potluck lists, church planning), rather than being pervasive throughout the day across all contexts. Patient explicitly denies anhedonia or persistent low mood outside of trigger-related situations, still enjoying yard work and family time, which argues against a major depressive episode. She also denies significant anxiety or being 'on edge,' pointing toward a predominantly depressed mood presentation rather than mixed anxiety/depression. The reaction is in excess of what would be expected given the stressor is functionally impairing (missing important commitments), meeting criteria for Adjustment Disorder with Depressed Mood rather than normal bereavement, which would not typically cause this degree of functional impairment or be diagnosed as a disorder.
